report:
## Research Findings

The evidence is more nuanced than a simple "false" — the claim is **partially true but conditional**, not simply false.

**Supporting mechanism:** Multiple controlled studies show that closed bedrooms accumulate CO2 (readings can exceed 2,500 ppm vs. ~650 ppm with a window/door open), and elevated CO2/poor ventilation correlates with reduced sleep quality and worse next-day cognitive performance. A well-cited Danish (DTU) field study of students sleeping with windows open vs. closed found improved air quality and better next-day performance, concluding that ventilation keeping CO2 below ~1,000 ppm supports "optimal sleep quality" (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459). A peer-reviewed study on bedroom air quality and sleep (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/) similarly found objective and subjective improvements in sleep and morning alertness with better ventilation.

**Important caveats:** The effect is context-dependent. The Sleep Foundation summary of a Shanghai study found that while opening windows improved objective air quality, actual sleep quality did *not* improve in summer conditions because open windows also let in heat and outdoor noise—offsetting the ventilation benefit (sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed). Aalto University research measuring CO2, temperature, and humidity with windows/doors open vs. closed likewise shows mixed subjective results depending on season and local conditions (research.aalto.fi).

## Conclusion
Rather than being false, the claim is **generally supported when ventilation lowers indoor CO2 without introducing excessive noise, cold, heat, or outdoor pollution**. In quiet, temperate, low-pollution settings, opening a window/door measurably improves air quality and sleep/cognitive metrics. In noisy, hot, cold, or polluted environments, the benefit can disappear or reverse. So: true under favorable conditions, not universally true.
